Data: [`churn.csv`](../materials/churn.csv), the split from Set 14, and the forest
from lecture 20, so that everyone explains the same model:

```{.r}
set.seed(17)
rf <- ranger(churn ~ ., data = train, num.trees = 300, probability = TRUE)
```

Before you start: `set.seed(17)` as above — the Blackboard test checks your
numbers against it. Your boosting model from Set 15 works for every question too;
only the numbers will differ.

## 1 · Partial dependence, and what it assumes

Compute the partial dependence of churn probability on `tenure_months`.

The curve is produced by averaging over the other columns *as if* they were
independent of tenure. Check that assumption here: `cor()` of `tenure_months`
with the numeric columns, and its mean by `contract`. Then name one column in a
*real* telecom table where the assumption would be plainly false, and say what
it would do to the shape you plotted.

## 2 · One customer, one explanation

Pick the held-out customer with the highest predicted churn probability.
Compute SHAP values for that single prediction.

Write the two-sentence explanation you would put in a retention agent's screen.
No jargon: the agent has ninety seconds before the call.

## 3 · Global and local disagree [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 21, on 11 Dec — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Compare the global importance ranking with the SHAP values for your chosen
customer.

They will not match. Explain why that is expected rather than a bug, and what
each one is actually a statement about.

## 4 · The counterfactual question

The manager asks: *"if we gave this customer a discount of 10 euro a month,
would they stay?"*

Use the model to answer, then write the caveat. The model was fitted on
observational data; say precisely what would have to be true for the number to
be a prediction of the intervention rather than an artefact of the fit.

## 5 · The model card [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 21, on 11 Dec — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Produce a half-page summary of your deployed model: what it predicts, on what
population, its test performance, the three variables that drive it, two
situations where it should not be trusted, and the date it should be refitted.

Someone must be able to read it without opening R.
